# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The expansion of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has driven demand for reliable large-bore vascular access. While transfemoral arterial access remains the default route for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), a substantial minority of patients have hostile iliofemoral anatomy precluding this approach [1,2]. Alternative access strategies—transapical, transaortic, transaxillary/subclavian, transcarotid, and transcaval—have been developed to serve these patients [3,4]. Transcaval access, in which the abdominal aorta is entered from the adjacent inferior vena cava (IVC), has emerged as a fully percutaneous, non-thoracic alternative that avoids the morbidity of surgical chest entry [5,6].

## Concept and Technique

Transcaval access exploits the close anatomic apposition of the IVC and abdominal aorta below the renal arteries [6]. A guidewire is electrified using an electrosurgical generator to cross from the cava into the aorta, after which a sheath is advanced over a stiff wire to deliver the device [5,7]. At completion, the aortocaval tract is closed with a nitinol occluder deployed across the defect [6,8]. The technique was pioneered in preclinical work demonstrating feasibility of catheter-based aortocaval crossing and closure [9], and translated into first-in-human procedures shortly thereafter [6]. Pre-procedural computed tomography is essential to identify a suitable calcium-free aortic target and to exclude interposed structures or large aortic aneurysm [10,11].

## Clinical Evidence

The seminal prospective multicenter Transcaval Access Study established procedural feasibility, reporting successful transcaval access in 99% of patients and successful TAVR delivery in the vast majority, despite a high-risk population unsuitable for transfemoral approaches [12]. Subsequent registry and single-center series confirmed reproducibility, with high rates of technical success and acceptable mortality given baseline risk [13,14]. Comparative analyses suggested that transcaval outcomes are competitive with, and in some series superior to, alternative non-femoral routes such as transapical and transaortic access, particularly regarding avoidance of thoracotomy-related complications [3,15].

Outcomes have improved with operator experience and refined patient selection [16]. The introduction of dedicated closure devices and standardized crossing protocols reduced bleeding events compared with early off-label use of cardiac occluders [8,17]. Registry data from experienced centers report 30-day mortality consistent with the comorbid TAVR population referred for alternative access [14,18].

## Complications and Management

The principal concern is bleeding from the aortocaval tract, which may manifest as retroperitoneal hematoma or, less commonly, hemodynamically significant extravasation [12,19]. Importantly, because pressure in the aorta exceeds that of the cava, residual flow often decompresses into the venous system, frequently producing a self-limiting aortocaval fistula rather than free retroperitoneal hemorrhage [12,20]. Most residual fistulae are small and either close spontaneously or remain clinically silent, though some require additional intervention with covered stents or repeat occluder placement [20,21]. Careful patient selection avoiding heavily calcified or aneurysmal target segments minimizes closure failure [10,11]. Vascular and access-site complications must be adjudicated using standardized VARC definitions to permit meaningful comparison across studies [22,23].

## Applications Beyond TAVR

Although developed primarily for TAVR, transcaval access has been applied to other large-bore interventions, including endovascular aneurysm repair in patients with prohibitive iliac anatomy and delivery of mechanical circulatory support devices [24,25]. The technique has also been explored as a route for transcatheter mitral and other structural interventions requiring substantial sheath caliber [26]. These extensions underscore transcaval access as a versatile platform for percutaneous delivery of bulky devices [5].

## Patient Selection and Future Directions

Optimal candidates have a calcium-free aortic crossing target adjacent to the IVC, below the renal arteries and above the aortic bifurcation [10,11]. Multidisciplinary heart-team evaluation integrating CT analysis is recommended to weigh transcaval access against other alternative routes such as transaxillary and transcarotid approaches, which have also matured considerably [4,27,28]. Ongoing device development, including purpose-built crossing and closure systems, is expected to further reduce complications and broaden adoption [17,29]. As transcatheter therapies extend to younger and more diverse populations, durable evidence comparing access strategies—ideally through randomized or large prospective registries—remains a priority [2,30].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access is a well-validated, fully percutaneous alternative for large-bore structural heart interventions in patients with unsuitable transfemoral anatomy. Supported by prospective multicenter data and growing registry experience, it offers a non-thoracic option with reproducible success and manageable, predominantly bleeding-related, complications. With refined selection and dedicated devices, transcaval access has secured a durable role within the contemporary structural intervention toolkit.
